title: Baseline retest for cores/bench
Serialize RV32M division to shorten the execute path
motivation:
The baseline's 199.8 ns, 156-cell critical path runs through forwarding and
the execute ALU. Four combinational 32-bit divide/remainder expressions are
present in that ALU; their long arithmetic chains are a likely Fmax limiter.
CoreMark should benefit from removing that chain even if each divide takes
multiple cycles, because divisions are much less frequent than ordinary ALU
operations.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the core's combinational DIV, DIVU, REM, and REMU datapaths with one
shared 32-step iterative unsigned divider. Capture forwarded operands at
launch, convert signed operands and results at the boundary, and implement
divide-by-zero and INT_MIN/-1 exactly. Hold the divide instruction in EX and
the younger fetch/decode state while it runs; drain older instructions and
inject invalid EX/MEM bubbles so no instruction retires twice. Complete the
divide only when the older MEM operation can advance, then resume normal
single-cycle issue. Keep the standalone combinational ALU behavior for its
direct unit tests and the RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS substitutes for formal checks,
while ensuring synthesis removes the unused combinational divider from core.
The shorter timed EX path should raise Fmax enough to outweigh divide stalls.

title: Eight-cycle divider removes the single-cycle EX critical path
motivation:
The baseline reaches only 5.442 MHz. Its 156-cell worst path runs from a
pipeline register through forwarding and the execute ALU to the data-memory
interface. The combinational 32-bit DIV/REM operators are a likely source
of that depth. Disassembly of the canonical 2K, -O3 CoreMark binary shows
only five DIVU instructions, all in main outside the start/stop timing
brackets; no DIV/REM instruction occurs in the measured kernels. Moving
division into a short iterative datapath should therefore raise Fmax
without adding divide cycles to the measured interval, and should also
reduce the baseline's 12,312 LUT4 footprint.

title: Early direct control-flow prediction with a small branch history table
motivation:
The existing IF stage always fetches PC+4 and waits for EX to resolve every
branch and jump. Each taken direct branch or JAL therefore discards a fetch
slot. CoreMark repeatedly executes loop branches, and its cycle count is
large enough that removing those redirect bubbles should improve iterations
per cycle without changing the divider-dominated Fmax path.

next PC with the instruction into EX; redirect and flush only when the
resolved architectural next PC differs. Train the branch table exactly once
when a valid branch advances from EX: instruction stalls can coexist with
training, while data stalls delay it until EX advances. Keep JALR on the
sequential path because its target needs a register operand.
A 32-entry table should capture hot CoreMark loops with modest LUT/FF cost.

title: Remove redirect feedback through fetch instruction and load-use hazard
motivation:
After iterative division raised Fmax to 41.009 MHz, the worst timed path
crosses execute redirect, fetch, load-use hazard, and the ID register input.
The fetch stage currently substitutes a NOP for every redirect, so the
branch decision fans through a 32-bit instruction mux before source-register
comparisons and ID stall/flush control. This feedback is unnecessary because
the redirected fetch is already invalidated by a dedicated ID flush.

title: Retopologize pipeline squashes around narrow valid bits
motivation:
The current 41.009 MHz champion has a 45-cell worst path reported from the
register file through ID, EX, IF, hazard logic, and back into the ID/EX
register. A redirect or instruction stall makes IF replace the entire
instruction with a NOP, so the execute-stage decision feeds instruction
decode and the load-use hazard network in the same cycle. It also clears
the whole ID/EX bundle. This control topology costs clock frequency on
every CoreMark cycle, while adding no useful work.

title: Compact branch history with one-bit prediction recovery
motivation:
The current iterative-divider core reaches 41.009 MHz, but every taken
branch and JAL still redirects from EX and flushes a fetched instruction.
The prior 32-entry branch-history experiment reduced CoreMark cycles from
4,491,485 to 4,203,502, showing useful control-flow locality; that attempt
ran on the old combinational-divider core, so its 5.366 MHz result does not
measure the present design. Reusing the measured two-bit direction predictor
while eliminating its 32-bit predicted-PC metadata targets the same cycle
savings with less register and correction logic on the current critical path.

in IF. Predict only validated conditional branch encodings with aligned
direct targets; predict aligned JAL taken and JALR sequentially. Form the
predicted target from the current fetched instruction and PC. Carry only
one predicted-taken bit through IF/ID and ID/EX, retaining it across stalls
and clearing it with bubbles. In EX, compare that bit with the actual branch
or jump outcome; redirect to PC+4 for a predicted-taken branch that is not

title: One-hot EX operand forwarding
motivation:
The champion's Gowin timing report has two nearly tied worst path classes:
register-file BSRAM through EX forwarding into branch recovery (27.579 ns),
and the same register-file/forwarding prefix through the multiplier to the
data-memory address (27.496 ns). Each forwarded operand currently passes
through three serial EX mux LUTs after the register-file read/bypass LUT.
Shortening the common prefix can improve both paths without changing IPC.

title: Register branch recovery at the EX/MEM boundary
motivation:
The current 112.36 fitness core is limited by a 46-cell path from the
register file through EX branch resolution, fetch, hazard logic, and back
to the ID/EX register. Earlier valid-bit squash restructuring alone moved
the bottleneck to the EX datapath but did not beat the champion. The
existing direction predictor removes most direct-branch corrections, so
one extra cycle on the remaining mispredictions should cost fewer CoreMark
cycles than the clock-frequency gain from breaking this feedback path.

title: Register predictor recovery before redirecting fetch
motivation:
The current predictor removes most taken-branch flushes, but its remaining
EX correction signal feeds back through IF and hazard logic into ID/EX.
Gowin reports that exact register-file-to-EX-to-IF-to-ID loop as the
27.579 ns critical path. A software model of its 32-entry counters over
the timed CoreMark instruction trace reports about 55,600 misses among
529,600 conditional branches; the trace also has 13,700 JALRs in 4.2
million measured cycles. Delaying their recovery by one cycle should cost
roughly 1.7% IPC, leaving room for a useful Fmax gain.

title: Register lookahead EX forwarding decisions
motivation:
The current 50.274 MHz critical path starts at the EX/MEM destination
register, passes through the forwarding comparison and EX operand mux,
then the ALU before reaching the EX/MEM register. Earlier one-hot operand
muxing regressed because it left the comparison on that same path. The
register addresses and producer controls are available a cycle before
the corresponding instruction reaches EX.

data memory, or division. With independent random instruction-bus stalls,
those lost fetch opportunities later become empty decode cycles. A prior

current EX retiming and its Fmax was limited by the old EX path.

title: Pack a sequential replay predictor into one block RAM
motivation:

motivation:

number of registered result sources while keeping adjacent dependencies

title: Retiming branch comparison and full multiplies into MEM
motivation:
The 223.78-fitness champion's worst path runs from an EX/MEM shift bank

product in MEM needs much less recombination and simpler stall accounting.

title: Banked 128-word sequential instruction replay
motivation:
The current 16-word replay table leaves many instruction-bus stalls exposed.
Earlier 256-word lookahead replay saved roughly 253,000 CoreMark cycles, but
its extra memory and routing reduced Gowin Fmax enough to lose fitness. A
64-word combinational table saved only about 131,000 cycles and also slowed
the PC-to-decode path. The useful direction is more replay coverage while
keeping a large table out of the same-cycle fetch and decode path.
